We were also usually escorted by the army. Therefore there is a probability that once they saw the soldiers, they opened fire. But in any case, fire was opened on us.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: How did you look at this incident? Did you see it as a provocation by the Croatian forces and was that their expression of a wish not to keep peace and destroy the truce?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, when there are bullets flying overhead, I can't say if it's a provocation or someone's trying to scare me off. But in any case, there seemed to have been an intentional attempt to cause that incident which would then cause the army to react. It was a regular occurrence that through such small incidents they were constantly provoking the army to react. With us, there was also a security major, Milutinovic, and Lieutenant Pecanac, as well as Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, witness. During the break I gave you a document which is 2D159. The Chamber is familiar with it. It is an excerpt from the book titled "Croatian homeland war." We will receive it in original form from the Croatian authorities. Did you have occasion to view it over the break? It's quite a lengthy document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did this one, but I didn't read the last two ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: We'll have time. And by the Chamber's leave, we'll discuss it tomorrow. We can now only comment upon one document. It refers to the 5th of April, 1991, when you were still not there. However, does it accurately reflect the conduct of the army in the area? This is an order for defence by the command of the 9th Corps whereby they order that the commands guard or keep safe the axes towards Knin, where some 3.000 members of the Croatian MUP are expected in the direction of Split, Knin, Vrlika, and Sibenik, as well as some auxiliary axes between Zadar, Obrovac, and Benkovac. Were all these directions in the direction of the Serb villages, and did the JNA, according to this order, exercise its duty to protect the Serb villages in preventing the Croatian forces to enter them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. The army moved its units, clearly indicating that it would not allow any violence or provocations against the population residing in the area. However, despite that, the provocations were frequent. Thanks to the army, the truce was enforce for at least some time. Had to not been for the army and its forces, I don't know what would have happened in that area. There would have been bloodshed. So in answer to your question: Yes, the army undertook all measures to prevent any further escalation of the tensions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Can we agree that the army in that period was the main, was the principal force in the area where you were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've been saying that all along. The army was the only relevant force in that area during that time. Only they could take any important action. There were no other such significant forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I'm looking at the clock, witness, and I have just one more question for today. It has to do with something an OTP witness stated. You said you were in Knin or in that area between May and October 1991; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you go to the Knin fortress?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you notice, there, any training camp for soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'll clarify. When we went to the Knin fortress, we were escorted by Lieutenant Pecanac from the army security service. We toured the entire fortress and found no camp, no army, or no uniformed personnel. There were a few tourists up there, but the soldiers didn't go up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you notice any offices, staffs, or anything of the sort?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. And we did tour it in detail. I just wanted to say the following: The lieutenant - what was his name? I just mentioned him - the one from the security service, we were kidding with him, asking him, All right, you can show us where the camp and the weapons are, and he took us through the entire fortress and found nothing. We found nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I have 30 seconds left. Let me finish this. Can you recall when it was when you went up to the fortress?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In August.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I close for the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bakrac. We will, as usual, adjourn in open session. Therefore, Witness DST-034, I'd like to instruct you that you should not speak to anyone or communicate in any other way with any other person about your testimony, whether that is testimony you've given today or whether that's testimony still to be given in the days to follow. I would invite you to follow the usher and would like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.00 in this same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We turn into open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. We'll adjourn for the day. And we'll resume tomorrow morning, Thursday, the 7th of July, 9.00, Courtroom II.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 7th day of July, 2011 at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: [Closed session]  [Confidentiality partially lifted by order of the Chamber]
--- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.48 p.m.,
